troph: feeding. auxotroph needs help, prototroph feeds itself.
oid: resembling but not the real thing.
postulate: a requirement that must be met before a claim counts as proven.
pathogen: a microbe that can cause disease.
virulent: able to cause disease. Avirulent means not able to.
virulence factor: any structure or product that helps cause disease: capsule, pili, toxins.
in vitro: in glass. A flask or plate, not a body.
strain: a genetic variant within one species.
serotype: a strain told apart by its surface antigens using antibodies.
antigen: any molecule an antibody can recognise.
phagocyte: an immune cell that eats microbes. Macrophages and neutrophils are phagocytes.
phagocytosis: the act of an immune cell swallowing a microbe.
macrophage: a large phagocyte. Literally big eater.
phenotype: what you can observe about a cell.
genotype: the genetic sequence behind the phenotype.
nucleoid: the unenclosed region holding the bacterial chromosome. Not a nucleus.
plasmid: small circular DNA that copies itself independently of the chromosome.
organelle: a membrane-wrapped compartment inside a cell. Bacteria have none.
sterol: a stiffening membrane lipid, cholesterol type. Bacteria lack them except Mycoplasma.
sedimentation: how fast a particle sinks when spun in a centrifuge. The S in 70S.
svedberg: the unit of sedimentation rate. The S number.
adhesin: a surface molecule used to stick to host cells. Pili carry them.
quorum sensing: genes switching on only once the population is dense enough, via secreted signals.
autoinducer: the secreted signal molecule that accumulates as a population grows.
biofilm: a community of bacteria glued into a protective slime matrix.
endospore: a dormant armored survival form made inside the cell.
germination: a spore waking back up into a growing cell.
vegetative cell: the normal growing dividing form, as opposed to a spore.
binary fission: one cell splitting into two identical cells. Bacterial reproduction.
peptidoglycan: the sugar and peptide mesh that forms the bacterial cell wall.
osmotic lysis: bursting because water rushed in. What the wall prevents.
turgor: the internal water pressure pushing outward on the wall.
mordant: a chemical that locks a dye in place. Iodine in the Gram stain.
decolouriser: the step that removes dye. Alcohol. The deciding step.
counterstain: the second dye colouring whatever lost the first. Safranin.
transpeptidase: the enzyme that cross-links wall peptides. Also called PBP.
pbp: penicillin binding protein. The transpeptidase that beta-lactams attack.
transglycosylase: the enzyme that links wall sugars into chains.
bactoprenol: the lipid carrier ferrying wall monomers across the membrane.
lysozyme: a tear and saliva enzyme that cuts the wall sugar backbone.
autolysin: the cell's own wall-cutting enzyme, used to make room for growth.
protoplast: a Gram positive cell stripped of its wall.
spheroplast: a Gram negative cell stripped of its peptidoglycan.
periplasm: the space between the two Gram negative membranes.
porin: a channel protein in the Gram negative outer membrane.
lps: lipopolysaccharide. The outer leaflet molecule of Gram negatives. Endotoxin.
lipid a: the toxic anchor portion of LPS. The actual endotoxin.
o antigen: the variable outer tip of LPS, used for serotyping.
endotoxin: LPS lipid A. Structural, Gram negative only, heat stable.
exotoxin: a secreted protein toxin. Heat labile, made by both Gram groups.
sepsis: a body-wide, dangerous response to infection.
septic shock: sepsis with collapse of blood pressure.
dic: disseminated intravascular coagulation. Clotting throughout the body at once.
acid-fast: holding stain despite an acid wash, thanks to waxy mycolic acids.
mycolic acid: the long waxy lipid of the mycobacterial wall.
teichoic acid: anionic polymer threaded through Gram positive wall. Positives only.
substrate: the molecule an enzyme works on.
substrate-level phosphorylation: making ATP by direct phosphate handoff, no ETC required.
fermentation: regenerating NAD+ by dumping electrons onto an organic molecule.
respiration: cashing in electrons through the ETC to a final acceptor.
etc: electron transport chain. The membrane relay that pumps protons.
proton motive force: the proton gradient across the membrane. Drives ATP synthase and flagella.
pmf: proton motive force. The proton gradient powering ATP synthase and flagella.
protonophore: a drug letting protons leak freely, collapsing the PMF.
final electron acceptor: whatever takes the electrons at the end. O2, nitrate, or an organic molecule.
amphibolic: a pathway that both breaks down and supplies building blocks. The TCA cycle.
generation time: the time for a population to double.
cfu: colony forming unit. One countable colony, assumed to come from one live cell.
turbidity: cloudiness of a culture. Measures total biomass, live plus dead.
serial dilution: repeated tenfold dilutions so colonies become countable.
selective medium: a medium that suppresses unwanted organisms so a target grows.
differential medium: a medium that makes different organisms look different.
fastidious: picky. Needing rich complex media to grow.
haemolysis: breaking red blood cells on blood agar. Alpha partial, beta complete.
siderophore: a secreted iron-grabbing molecule. Counters the host hiding its iron.
prototroph: a cell that can make all its own growth factors. Wild type.
auxotroph: a mutant needing a specific nutrient supplied.
mic: minimum inhibitory concentration. Lowest dose that stops growth.
mbc: minimum bactericidal concentration. Lowest dose that kills.
spectrum: the range of organisms a drug touches. Broad or narrow.
selective toxicity: hurting the microbe while sparing the host.
therapeutic index: toxic dose divided by effective dose. Higher is safer.
beta-lactam: the drug family sharing the four-membered ring that mimics D-Ala-D-Ala.
beta-lactamase: a bacterial enzyme that destroys the beta-lactam ring.
synergy: two drugs helping each other, more than the sum.
antagonism: two drugs getting in each other's way.
prodrug: a drug inactive until converted. Isoniazid is one.
efflux pump: a membrane pump that throws drug back out of the cell.
intrinsic resistance: resistance built into the species by nature.
acquired resistance: resistance gained by mutation or gene transfer.
ototoxic: poisonous to the ears, causing hearing loss.
neutropenic: short on neutrophils. An immune system that cannot finish the job.
empiric: treating on best guess, before culture results come back.
bacteriostatic: stops growth without killing. Needs the immune system to finish.
replicon: any DNA molecule with its own origin, able to replicate itself.
oric: the fixed start point of bacterial chromosome replication.
semiconservative: each daughter helix keeps one old strand and one new one.
primer: a short RNA starter giving polymerase a free 3 prime end to build from.
primase: the enzyme that lays down RNA primers.
helicase: the enzyme that unzips the double helix.
ligase: the enzyme that seals a nick by forming the missing bond.
processivity: how long an enzyme keeps working without falling off.
exonuclease: an enzyme that chews nucleotides from an end. Used in proofreading.
gap: missing nucleotides in a strand. Pol I fills it.
nick: a missing bond only, all nucleotides present. Ligase seals it.
okazaki fragment: a short piece of the lagging strand, made away from the fork.
promoter: the DNA site where RNA polymerase binds to start.
operator: the DNA site where a repressor binds to block.
holoenzyme: the complete enzyme. Core polymerase plus sigma.
core enzyme: RNA polymerase without sigma. Can write but cannot find the start.
sigma: the subunit that finds promoters. Gives specificity, not catalysis.
transcript: the RNA copy produced by transcription.
polycistronic: one mRNA carrying several genes. The operon's product.
operon: one promoter controlling a cluster of genes as a single unit.
inducible: normally off. A signal turns it on. Catabolic, like lac.
repressible: normally on. A signal turns it off. Anabolic, like trp.
inducer: a molecule that inactivates a repressor, turning genes on.
corepressor: a molecule that activates a repressor, turning genes off.
allolactose: the true inducer of the lac operon, an isomer of lactose.
constitutive: always expressed. Regulation lost or absent.
attenuation: cutting transcription short using the leader sequence. Used by trp.
catabolite repression: glucose lowering cAMP so CAP cannot activate the lac operon.
shine-dalgarno: the mRNA sequence that pairs with 16S rRNA to position the ribosome.
ribozyme: an RNA that acts as an enzyme. Peptidyl transferase is one.
mutagen: an agent that raises the mutation rate.
carcinogen: an agent that causes cancer. Ames links mutagens to carcinogens.
revertant: a mutant whose phenotype has returned to wild type.
transition: a base swap of like for like. Purine to purine.
transversion: a base swap across types. Purine to pyrimidine.
missense: a mutation giving a different amino acid.
nonsense: a mutation giving a premature stop codon.
silent: a base change with no amino acid change.
frameshift: an insertion or deletion that shifts the reading frame.
wild type: the standard, unmutated form of an organism.
intercalating agent: a flat molecule that wedges between bases, causing frameshifts.
base analogue: a fake base that gets incorporated then mispairs.
deamination: removing an amino group from a base. What nitrous acid does.
pyrimidine dimer: two adjacent pyrimidines fused by UV light, blocking replication.
fluctuation test: the Luria-Delbruck experiment showing mutations arise before selection.
ames test: a test for mutagenicity, counting revertant colonies of a histidine auxotroph.
horizontal gene transfer: DNA moving between cells rather than parent to offspring.
competence: the state of being able to take up naked DNA from outside.
naked dna: free DNA in the environment, with no cell or capsid around it.
transformation: uptake of naked DNA by a competent cell. DNase destroys it.
transduction: DNA transfer carried inside a bacteriophage particle.
conjugation: DNA transfer requiring cell contact through a pilus.
capsid: the protein shell of a virus.
lytic: the phage cycle that multiplies and bursts the host cell.
lysogenic: the phage cycle where the genome hides inside the host.
prophage: phage DNA integrated and sitting quietly in the host chromosome.
temperate phage: a phage that can choose lytic or lysogenic.
lysogenic conversion: a prophage giving its host a new trait, usually a toxin.
f factor: the fertility plasmid encoding the sex pilus and transfer genes.
hfr: high frequency of recombination. An F factor integrated into the chromosome.
f prime: an F factor that excised sloppily, carrying chromosomal genes with it.
merodiploid: partially diploid. Carrying two copies of some genes.
transposon: a jumping element that moves between DNA molecules but cannot self-replicate.
transposase: the enzyme a transposon uses to jump.
insertion sequence: the simplest transposon, carrying only transposase.
integron: a platform that captures and expresses resistance gene cassettes.
dnase: an enzyme that destroys free DNA. The test that identifies transformation.
interrupted mating: an experiment mapping genes by their time of entry during conjugation.
replica plating: pressing colonies onto new plates to compare growth on different media.
minimal medium: a medium with only the bare essentials. Auxotrophs cannot grow on it.
